title: FlashNext-RL: A System Optimization Study for Long-Horizon Agentic RL of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next
trick: Fit a 125B mixture-of-experts agent's RL trainer on one 8-GPU node by pinning offloaded state in exact-size arenas, keeping expert gradients on the GPU, and hand-writing the model's sparse-attention, expert and residual kernels.
framing_stripped: Called 'FlashNext-RL, a model-specific RL training optimization framework'; it is an engineering log of fitting one 125B-parameter model (6B active, plus a frozen 51B n-gram table) into a 2 TB host-memory and 8 x 179 GiB GPU budget for 131K-token SWE rollouts, with a controlled add-one-at-a-time ablation ladder run only on a truncated 8-layer copy of the model (Table 10), uncontrolled development snapshots on the full model (Table 12, caption: 'not a controlled speedup comparison'), and an 11-step live run (steps 5-15, Table 16) that reports iteration time but no task accuracy.
method_equations: Memory arithmetic that forces the layout (sec. 1, 3.1). Checkpointed residual stream per GPU without context parallelism: $M_{\text{act}} = L \cdot T \cdot d \cdot 2\,\text{bytes}$ with $L = 48$ layers, $T = 131{,}072$ tokens, $d = 10{,}240$ (the 4-branch residual stream of width $4 \times 2560$), giving $M_{\text{act}} \approx 129$ GB. Host memory under CPU offload: $M_{\text{host}} = b \cdot P$ with $P \approx 129 \times 10^9$ parameters and $b = 16$ bytes/param for AdamW (fp32 master, fp32 gradient, two fp32 moments) or $b = 12$ for the Muon budget (one moment), i.e. 1,922 GiB vs 1,442 GiB before the 95.4 GiB n-gram table on a node with 1,937 GiB available (Table 2). Muon update scaling: an $A \times B$ matrix's orthogonalized update is multiplied by $0.2\sqrt{\max(A,B)}$ so its RMS matches AdamW's. Throughput metric (sec. 3.1): $\text{REAL} = \frac{N_{\text{np}}}{t_{\text{step}} \cdot 8}$ tokens/s/GPU, with $N_{\text{np}}$ the non-padding tokens in a step and $t_{\text{step}}$ its wall time, averaged over steady steps. Model FLOPs per token: $6P_m$ per trainable matrix with $P_m$ weights (forward plus backward), summed over the active path, plus sparse-attention products, indexer scores and a GDN-recurrence estimate; this is 40.3 GFLOP/token unfrozen, 39.1 with two layers frozen, 8.2 for the 8-layer model; hardware FLOPs add checkpoint recompute; matmul-only hardware cost is 48.4 GFLOP/token. Live iteration time (sec. 5, Table 16): $t_{\text{iter}} = t_{\text{wait}} + t_{\text{fwd/bwd}} + t_{\text{load}} + t_{\text{Muon}} + t_{\text{bcast}}$, with means $331 + 964 + 10 + 12 + 19 \approx 1{,}344$ s; the wait term is the trainer idling for rollouts, so the loop is generation-bound by $331/1{,}344 = 25\%$. Capacity extrapolation (sec. 5): with slowdown proxy $s \in [7.4, 10.4]$ (8-layer ladder ratio $17{,}678/2{,}391$; full-model $4{,}438/426$) and assumed linear scaling, the stock trainer needs $s \cdot 1{,}013\,\text{s} / 1{,}344\,\text{s} \approx 8$ to $11$ training nodes to match one optimized node.
load_bearing_assumption: That the measured throughput is attributable to the named optimizations rather than to the configuration changes bundled with them: the full-model endpoints (395 to 4,438 REAL tokens/s/GPU) switch bin size from 32K to 131K, batch from 16 samples (1.1M tokens) to 7.1-7.6M tokens, and CP from 1 to 4 across rows (Table 12 caption), and the controlled ladder exists only on an 8-layer model whose FLOP mix differs (output head is 19% of its FLOPs vs 4% at 48 layers; footnote 1). Second, that freezing the first two layers, the sparse-attention indexer, the n-gram table and the MTP head, plus BF16 with router replay, trains the same policy a full-parameter trainer would; the paper's only evidence is bounded entropy (0.66-0.76 nats/token) and mismatch KL (3.6-4.0e-3) over 11 steps, and it states it 'does not establish long-run convergence or task-quality improvement' (sec. 5, 6).
weakest_component: The headline speedup is not a controlled measurement. The 10.4x full-model ratio (426 to 4,438 REAL tokens/s/GPU, Table 12) changes batch size and settings between rows, and the authors say so; the 7.4x controlled ladder (Table 10) is on 8 of 48 layers, keeps the full 248K-vocabulary output head (19% of its FLOPs), does not freeze its first two layers, and its baseline L0 already contains seven 'cannot be turned off' correctness fixes (footnote 2), so the stock-vs-optimized gap is understated in one place and the kernel shares overstated in another (fused glue: +3.2% on 8 layers, +0.7% on the full model, sec. 3.2.9). Second target: the live run is 11 reported steps of a single configuration (one 8xB200 training node, three inference nodes), no accuracy, no second model, no multi-node point; the 8-11 training-node capacity claim (sec. 5) is an extrapolation that assumes linear scaling of a trainer the authors note was host-copy-bound. Third: the loop is declared 'bound by generation' (trainer waits 331 of 1,344 s on average, 702 s at step 14), but the generation side has about a third of its 112 sessions per engine idle waiting on sandbox commands at any time (77 of 112 generating, sec. 2.3), and the paper says these measurements 'do not isolate' the sandbox contribution from GPU limits, so the binding resource of the whole loop is not actually identified.
regime: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next: 125B parameters, 6B active per token (512 experts per layer, top-10, intermediate 640), 36 Gated DeltaNet linear-attention layers plus 12 Qwen Sparse Attention layers (indexer selects up to 512 blocks of 4 keys per query), a 4-branch gated residual stream (width 10,240), a frozen 51B-parameter n-gram embedding table (95.4 GiB BF16), a 4B multi-token-prediction head used for 3-token speculative decoding (sec. 1). Hardware: four 8xB200 nodes (179 GiB per GPU, 192 cores, about 2.0 TB host memory each, 8x400 Gb/s EFA), one for training, three for inference (6 vLLM 0.31 engines, TP 4 + EP, 112 sessions each, 672 rollouts in flight). Task: SWE rollouts via prime-rl and verifiers, one Kubernetes sandbox pod per rollout, total context capped at 131,072 tokens (one training bin); median rollout 29K tokens, p90 61K, p99 108K, 7.7% of rollouts over 64K hold 19% of tokens (Fig. 4). Batch: 1,024 trainable rollouts per step, collected 1,249-1,584 (mean 1,393) because zero-advantage groups are discarded; about 36.5M packed tokens per step. Speed: trainer 4,438 REAL tokens/s/GPU in replay (213 matmul TFLOPs/GPU), 4,737 packed tokens/s/GPU live; generation 17.1K output tokens/s across 24 GPUs (about 710 per GPU); iteration 1,344 s (22.4 min) mean, 1,137-1,690 s range; weight broadcast of about 260 GB BF16 takes 18.6 s; checkpoint step 102 s (DCP 923 GB to local NVMe in 70 s). Stability window: steps 5-15 only; entropy 0.66-0.76 nats/token; trainer-sampler mismatch KL 3.6-4.0e-3 with router replay. No pass rate or task accuracy reported.
information_asymmetry: Five concrete asymmetries, each with the stage where the information lives. (1) Inference vs trainer, expert routing: two BF16 implementations pick different top-10 experts for the same token, and these routing flips explain about 96% of trainer-inference mismatch in the authors' offline measurement (sec. 2.2); the inference engine knows which experts it used, the trainer by default does not, so the fix is to ship the routes (a [T, 48, 10] uint16 tensor, 960 bytes per token, about 37 GB per 39M-token batch) and replay them; the paper reports the resulting KL (3.6-4.0e-3) but never the KL without replay on this model, so the size of the asymmetry on this model is asserted from an offline measurement, not shown live. (2) Orchestrator vs generation, trainable-group status: whether a prompt's group of rollouts carries signal (not all rewards equal) is known only after every rollout in the group finishes, yet all are generated at full cost; in steps 5-15, 1,393 rollouts were collected per step to obtain 1,026 trainable ones, so 26% of generated rollouts (and their sandbox time) are thrown away every step (Table 16), and the paper neither predicts group outcome early nor accounts for the discarded tokens in its throughput figures. (3) Engine vs sandbox: at any time about 35 of 112 sessions per engine are between turns waiting for a sandbox command (sec. 2.3); the engine admits sessions by KV-cache usage (cap at 65%, resume below 55%) with no knowledge of command durations, and the paper states it does not isolate the sandbox's share of unused serving capacity from GPU limits; a per-turn timeline of generate vs execute per rollout exists in the orchestrator logs and was not reported. (4) Hindsight vs forward, rollout length: the trainer packs rollouts into fixed 131K bins and the orchestrator caps context at 131K; the length distribution (median 29K, p99 108K) is known only after generation, so padding inside bins is paid at training time (4,737 packed vs about 4,438 non-padding tokens/s/GPU, two numbers the authors say are not directly comparable), and the loop's 25% trainer wait is set by the tail of the collection, not the median (wait 186-702 s across steps). (5) Development time vs live time: static expert placement is fit from 'a few real steps' recorded before the run (max/mean load 1.233 to 1.059), the MTP draft head is frozen while the policy moves (acceptance 1.82-1.88 in replay, 2.55 live, and the authors expect decay over a long run and 'monitor it'), and the ladder's kernel shares are measured on 8 layers; whether routing load, draft acceptance and kernel shares drift as the policy trains is information that only a longer live run holds, and the run reported is 11 steps. For L3 the actionable asymmetry is (2) plus (3): the true cost per trainable rollout in this loop is the generated-but-discarded 26%, the sandbox-idle third of session slots, and the 25% trainer wait, three measured waste terms the paper reports separately and never adds up into a cost structure.
occupies: The single-node BF16 recipe for RL-training Qwen3.8-Flash-Next in prime-rl: exact-size pinned host arenas for FSDP2 offload (Muon step 75 s to 12.4 s), GPU-resident expert gradients across micro steps (2.4-2.7x), a Mixture-of-Kittens fork with native intermediate size 640 and 52/52 communication SMs, GQA-native sparse-attention kernels with a CuTe dK/dV at 46.7 ms per layer at 64K, fused gated-residual read/inject (1.95x over torch.compile, 8x less kept memory), a GPU UVA gather from a tmpfs-mapped 95 GiB n-gram table, router replay through vLLM's auxiliary output, layer-by-layer bounded weight broadcast, and checkpoint export from the broadcast's gathered layers; plus the 8-layer cumulative ladder (2,391 to 17,678 REAL tokens/s/GPU) and the host-memory accounting (PSS not RSS; Table 13, Table 14) for a 1,024-rollout, 131K-context SWE run on 4x8 B200.

neighbors.title: AReaL: A Large-Scale Asynchronous Reinforcement Learning System for Language Reasoning
neighbors.trick: Decouple generation from training completely: rollout workers never wait for the batch's longest output, training updates whenever a batch is ready, and a staleness-aware PPO variant absorbs the outdated samples, for up to 2.77x speedup over synchronous RL; this card's paper keeps a per-step batch and instead attacks the trainer's memory and kernels for one model.

neighbors.title: HybridFlow: A Flexible and Efficient RLHF Framework (verl)
neighbors.trick: Express RL post-training as a dataflow with a single controller for the graph and multi-controllers inside each node, plus a 3D engine that reshards the actor between training and generation with no duplicated memory; the general-purpose infrastructure that this card's paper says does not by itself solve a model-specific 131K single-node target.

neighbors.title: Stabilizing MoE Reinforcement Learning by Aligning Training and Inference Routers (R3)
neighbors.trick: Record which experts the inference engine routed each token to and replay those routes in the trainer, removing the training-inference policy KL that routing flips cause and preventing MoE RL collapse; this card's paper adopts exactly this and finds routing flips explain about 96% of its mismatch.

neighbors.title: Mixture-of-Kittens: MoE Megakernel for NVL72s
neighbors.trick: Fuse token dispatch, routed and shared expert FFNs and token combine into one deterministic persistent kernel that picks push or pull communication per operator and removes all CPU-GPU synchronization, for up to 2.37x the best public MoE layer throughput on a scale-up fabric; this card's paper forks it to drop the padding of its 640-wide experts to 768.

neighbors.title: INTELLECT-3: Technical Report
neighbors.trick: Train a 106B MoE (12B active) with large-scale asynchronous RL on an open stack (prime-rl, verifiers, environments hub) scaling to 512 H200s with multi-turn tool use built in; prime-rl is the trainer and orchestrator this card's paper builds on and then specializes to one architecture on one node.

theme_fit.why: directly answers the lane sentence: rollout engine configuration (TP/EP, KV admission, prefix-cache hit 85%), asynchronous-ish trainer/generator overlap with a measured 25% trainer wait, sandbox-state costs (238 MB harness tarball, kubectl memory), and the per-step time and memory accounting of a real long-horizon SWE RL loop
same words (long-horizon agent RL, entropy, trainer-sampler KL, router replay) but the paper fixes stability by systems means and reports no training dynamics or credit result; 11 steps, no accuracy
supplies raw cost-accounting numbers for agentic training (collected vs trained rollouts, rollout length tail, sandbox idle share) but no evaluation instrument and no agent measurement

limitations_as_complaints: My run is 11 reported steps on one hardware configuration; I cannot say whether the frozen first two layers, frozen indexer, frozen MTP head and BF16 router replay change what the policy learns, because I never measured task accuracy or long-run convergence, only that entropy stayed in 0.66-0.76 and mismatch KL in 3.6-4.0e-3 (sec. 5 'Stability'; sec. 6).

I cannot tell you a controlled end-to-end speedup for the full model: my 395 to 4,438 tokens/s/GPU endpoints change bin size, batch size and CP between rows, my controlled ladder is on an 8-layer model whose output head is 19% of FLOPs, and my 8-11 node capacity estimate assumes linear scaling I never measured (Table 12 caption; footnote 1; sec. 5 'Illustrative capacity estimate').

A quarter of my iteration is the trainer waiting for rollouts, a third of my engine sessions are idle waiting on sandbox commands, and a quarter of the rollouts I generate are discarded as zero-advantage groups, yet I did not isolate the sandbox's share of unused serving capacity from GPU limits and I report no per-turn generate-vs-execute timeline (sec. 2.3; sec. 5 'Speed'; Table 16).
